The oval butterflyfish, Chaetodon lunulatus, is a common coral reef species across the Indo-Pacific. Reared in controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], the embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with eggs hatching into yolk-sac larvae after approximately 1.25 days [ab = approximately 1.25 days]. This brief incubation period is typical for small, pelagic eggs; the newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic and depend entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves. The wet weight of newly hatched individuals is estimated from the egg diameter of 0.75 mm, yielding a value of approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams]. This minute initial mass reflects the energetic constraints of producing numerous small, transparent eggs characteristic of broadcast-spawning teleosts. The onset of first exogenous feeding occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, marking the transition to an actively feeding, planktonic larval phase that will eventually recruit to bentic habitats.

Growth in the wild proceeds steadily throughout the juvenile phase, with individuals attaining a total length at puberty of 8.2 centimeters [Lp = 8.2 centimeters]. This measurement corresponds to the size at which gonadal differentiation and reproductive maturation are typically initiated, a stage often linked to the occupation of stable territories on the reef. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from the length-weight relationship for this species, is 12.6 grams [Wwp = 12.6 grams]. This value is comparatively low among butterflyfishes, reflecting the relatively small size at which C. lunulatus initiates gametogenesis. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, adults continue to grow, albeit at a decelerating rate, ultimately approaching a maximum or ultimate total length of 26.7 centimeters [Li = 26.7 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is achieved only after several years of sustained somatic investment.

The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum recorded length is 436 grams [Wwi = 436 grams], a value calculated from the species-specific length-weight conversion factor. This adult body mass is consistent with a moderately sized Chaetodon species of the family Chaetodontidae that maintains a corallivorous diet. Lifespan estimates under natural thermal regimes, particularly at the typical reef temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 9,125 days [am = approximately 9,125 days]. This translates to about 25 years, placing C. lunulatus among the longer-lived members of its genus. Such extended lifespans are often associated with low natural mortality rates in the adult stage and a relatively stable environment on coral reefs. The species demonstrates an iteroparous reproductive strategy, spawning multiple times across its long adult life, which buffers against years of poor recruitment.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) is the proportion of body mass made up of gonad tissue. For C. lunulatus the GSI was 6% [GSI = 6%] at a water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This moderate index suggests that reproductive effort, while significant, does not dominate somatic mass, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy that spreads reproductive output across multiple seasons. A gravid female thus allocates roughly 6% of her wet weight to developing oocytes during the spawning period. This allocation is likely influenced by local food availability, as access to preferred coral prey can modulate the energetic reserves available for vitellogenesis. This value of 6% [GSI = 6%] represents a mean for reproductively active individuals across populations at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C].

Comparing these life-history metrics with those of congeneric species reveals several distinctive features within the family Chaetodontidae. The total length at puberty of 8.2 centimeters [Lp = 8.2 centimeters] is reached relatively early, allowing young adults to participate in spawning aggregations sooner than some larger congeners that delay maturation until reaching a greater size. The wet weight at birth of 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams] is typical of pelagic-spawning chaetodontids, whose small egg size facilitates wide dispersal via ocean currents. The maximum lifespan of 9,125 days [am = 9,125 days] at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] is notable, as it exceeds the documented longevity of several other butterflyfish species with similar body sizes. This extended lifespan, coupled with the age at birth of 1.25 days [ab = 1.25 days], underscores a life-history strategy that emphasizes adult survival and repeated reproductive events over a prolonged adult phase, a pattern well-suited to the relatively predictable but patchy resources of coral reef ecosystems at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C].
